clue.text: A cross can't come to grief — it's inviolable

indicators.note: to come to grief is to be wrecked, so the letters of the words before it are smashed and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A crucifix that cannot be damaged is something holy and untouchable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'come to grief' rearranges the letters of A CROSS CANT; the apostrophe in can't adds no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sacred and beyond criticism or violation is held inviolable.

clue.text: As previously described, silver is hidden inside pudding…

indicators.note: the metal is tucked within the other word, so these words signal one piece placed inside another

parts.note: so means thus, in the manner already stated
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A coin buried in a pudding, as mentioned before.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs this clue on into the next, which continues the pudding theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A milk pudding made from palm-starch granules is a classic British nursery dessert.

clue.text: … with firm approval of chef

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm
OK is an expression of approval

explanation.surface: Continuing the pudding: it comes with the chef's firm seal of approval.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this to the pudding clue above, but the clue stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A chef is a professional kitchen worker who prepares food, a synonym.

clue.text: One will probably use all the rests, working on a big score

definitions.text: One will probably use all the rests, working on a big score

parts.words: One will probably use all the rests, working on a big score
parts.note: a score is a full musical part-book for many players, and its rests are the silent beats; the person arranging it for a full band uses them all

explanation.surface: Someone who takes every break while chasing a huge win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rests' and 'score' look like idleness and winnings, but both are musical: silent beats and the written music for an ensemble.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who arranges music for the instruments of a large ensemble writes out every part, rests included.

clue.text: Early author's article on reversal of attitude

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece sitting on another comes first, above it

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

indicators.note: reversal tells us the word for attitude is read backwards

parts.note: a pose is an attitude, a bodily stance

explanation.surface: An old writer's essay on changing one's stance.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the article above the turned word, so it comes first; 'reversal of' turns the word for attitude backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek fabulist of the sixth century BC is among the earliest named writers of moral tales.

clue.text: Shift is detailed to attempt this mysterious process

indicators.note: de-tailed means having its tail cut off, so the last letter of the garment goes

parts.note: a shift is a loose dress or slip, also called a chemise
to try is to attempt

explanation.surface: A worker on a shift is assigned to try out some puzzling procedure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' reads as 'assigned' to a task but means de-tailed: the garment loses its final letter. 'this' and 'to' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Chemistry is used for the inexplicable attraction or interaction between people, an elusive process.

clue.text: Hear athlete is puffed

indicators.note: hear asks us to take the sound of the word for athlete rather than its spelling

parts.note: a Blue is a sportsperson who has represented Oxford or Cambridge University

explanation.surface: Listen: the runner is out of breath.
explanation.walkthrough: A Blue is an Oxford or Cambridge sportsperson, so named for the university colours.
explanation.definitionFit: Puffed is the past tense of puff, to exhale a gust of breath or wind.

clue.text: The daily habit of a kind of lizard?

definitions.text: The daily habit of a kind of lizard?

parts.words: The daily habit of a kind of lizard?
parts.note: a lounge lizard is a idle man-about-town, and habit is used in its clothing sense: what he wears every day

explanation.surface: A question about the routine behaviour of some reptile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'habit' means clothing, as a monk's habit; a lounge lizard is a man who idles in fashionable bars, dressed for the part.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's ordinary business outfit of matching jacket and trousers is everyday wear, not formal dress.

clue.text: Why was I shy, awkward and thin?

indicators.note: awkward means clumsily arranged, so these letters are shuffled into new order

explanation.surface: Someone wonders why they were so bashful and gauche.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkward' rearranges the letters of WHY WAS I SHY.
explanation.definitionFit: Wishy-washy describes something feeble, watery or lacking substance, like thin soup.

clue.text: He's in poor shape when opening play? Hard cheese!

definitions.text: He's in poor shape when opening play?

explanation.surface: A complaint about a misshapen actor at the start of a show, met with a curt 'bad luck'.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Richard III opens with the soliloquy of the hunchbacked Duke of this title; Double Gloucester is a hard English cheese, and 'hard cheese!' is British slang for bad luck.
explanation.definitionFit: The deformed duke speaks the opening lines of Shakespeare's Richard III, and the same county name labels a firm English cheese.

clue.text: This hospital will admit dolls, too

definitions.text: This hospital will admit dolls, too

parts.words: This hospital will admit dolls, too
parts.note: a London teaching hospital whose name, without the apostrophe, pairs with dolls in the title of a Broadway musical

explanation.surface: A hospital that will take in toy patients as well.
explanation.walkthrough: The London hospital founded by Thomas Guy shares its name with the musical Guys and Dolls; it would 'admit' dolls into its title.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous London hospital's name also means men or fellows, matched with dolls in the musical title.

clue.text: Herb no longer tended — that's foolish

parts.note: a simple is an archaic name for a medicinal herb, so no longer marks an outdated word
minded means looked after or tended

explanation.surface: A herb garden left untended is a silly idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no longer' flags an archaic sense: in old usage a simple was a medicinal plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking intelligence or sense is a synonym for being foolish.

clue.text: Literary giant lying drunk hopelessly so

parts.note: Giant Despair is the ogre of Doubting Castle in Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress

indicators.note: drunk means tipsy and reeling, so the letters of the next word are jumbled

explanation.surface: A great writer is lying in a hopelessly drunken state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literary giant' suggests a great author, but it is a real giant in a book. 'drunk' turns LYING into INGLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting without any hope is the same as acting in a manner that has given up hope.

clue.text: One needs a breather to read volumes

definitions.text: One needs a breather to read volumes

parts.words: One needs a breather to read volumes
parts.note: a breather is someone blowing into the device, and the volumes are lung capacities measured, not books

explanation.surface: Someone who must take a rest before tackling more books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breather' suggests a rest and 'volumes' books, but the device needs a person to breathe into it and it reads air volumes.
explanation.definitionFit: A medical instrument that measures how much air the lungs take in and expel is used by a patient blowing into it.

clue.text: Light-hearted wild antics in Open University, kept to a minimum?

indicators.note: wild means unruly and out of control, so the pooled letters are thrown into a new order

parts.words: Open University, kept to a minimum
parts.note: kept to a minimum means cut down to its initials, so the Open University becomes OU

explanation.surface: Carefree students get up to riotous behaviour at a low-key distance-learning college.
explanation.walkthrough: The Open University is Britain's distance-learning university. 'wild' scrambles ANTICS, IN and OU together.
explanation.definitionFit: Being nonchalant and free from worry is the same as being carefree and cheerful.

clue.text: Being so boring, it reduces tension in retorts

explanation.surface: A dull person defuses arguments by being tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' means drilling into, not dull; 'retorts' are laboratory flasks, not sharp replies, and the tension is a liquid's surface tension.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that pierces or soaks in is penetrating; such a wetting agent lowers liquid surface tension in chemistry flasks.

clue.text: Not believing He is in the highest place?

indicators.note: in places the two words He is inside the word for the top room

parts.note: an attic is the room at the top of a house

explanation.surface: Doubting whether God is in heaven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' reads as God and 'the highest place' as heaven, but it is the top floor of a house.
explanation.definitionFit: Denying that any god exists is a refusal of religious belief.

clue.text: Forgotten article found in tagliatelle, say

parts.note: past means over and done with, gone and forgotten
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A lost item discovered in a plate of noodles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' only links the wordplay to the definition here, not an insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: Tagliatelle is one example of Italian noodle dough cut into shapes.

clue.text: Painter holding coal-scuttle is a girl…

indicators.note: holding means one piece wraps round another

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword stock painter
a hod is a coal-scuttle as well as a builder's carrier

explanation.surface: An artist clutches a coal bucket: a young woman's picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this to the next clue's surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A female given name, so a girl may be called this.

clue.text: …sort of dishy one Henry is attached to, yet unladylike

indicators.note: attached to means the letter is fixed on at the end
sort here means to arrange, so the letters of the following words are rearranged

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: An attractive girl whom Henry is fond of, though she is rough-mannered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges DISHY ONE into HOYDENIS, and H follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoyden is a boisterous tomboy, so behaving like one lacks feminine decorum.

clue.text: Current course that comes with tiniest of chips?

definitions.text: Current course that comes with tiniest of chips?

parts.words: Current course that comes with tiniest of chips?
parts.note: an electrical path for flowing charge, built on the smallest silicon chips

explanation.surface: A menu: the latest course, served with the smallest chips.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current course' suggests the dish now being served and 'chips' fried potatoes; here they are electricity's route and silicon.
explanation.definitionFit: An integrated electronic circuit made at tiny scale sits on a semiconductor chip.

clue.text: Music-maker for the sitting-bower

parts.note: a bower is read as one who bows, and this string player draws a bow while seated

explanation.surface: Something to make music in a garden arbour where people sit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bower' looks like a leafy shelter but means someone using a bow, and this instrument is played seated.
explanation.definitionFit: A large bowed string instrument held between the knees is played by a seated performer.

clue.text: Inadequate tip?

explanation.surface: A complaint that a gratuity was too small.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tip' looks like a gratuity but means to tilt.
explanation.definitionFit: Lean means meagre or scanty, and also to tilt or incline to one side.

clue.text: Man, for example, is left a foot short

indicators.note: short means lacking, so the word for left is missing the abbreviation for foot

parts.note: ft is the abbreviation for a foot, the unit of length

explanation.surface: A man left with only one foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea, not a person. 'short' removes FT from LEFT, leaving LE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is an example of a small island.

clue.text: Cheeky drop in rent

explanation.surface: An impudent fall in what a tenant pays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheeky' suggests impudence but means on the cheek; 'rent' is a rip, not a payment.
explanation.definitionFit: A drop of liquid running down the cheek from the eye, and a rip in cloth, share this spelling.

clue.text: This state provides exhibition of very little interest

definitions.text: This state provides exhibition of very little interest

parts.words: This state provides exhibition of very little interest
parts.note: a condition of being impassive, which shows hardly any curiosity or emotion

explanation.surface: A country stages a show nobody cares about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'state' reads as a nation and 'exhibition' as a show, but they are a condition and a display of feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: Being stolid means being dull and unemotional, displaying almost no curiosity.

clue.text: Formal procedure correctly reported

indicators.note: reported means spoken aloud, so the word for correctly is taken by its sound

parts.note: right means correctly, as in doing it right

explanation.surface: A ceremony was described accurately.
explanation.definitionFit: A rite is a ceremonial act performed according to set custom.

clue.text: Giving concert?

explanation.surface: Putting on a musical performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concert' looks like a performance but means agreement, as in acting 'in concert'.
explanation.definitionFit: Accordance means the act of granting, from accord, to give, and also harmony or agreement.
